meta.subject: other
meta.description: CS fundamentals: data types, algorithms, Big O, sorting, binary/hex, boolean logic, variables, loops, conditionals, functions, debugging, internet basics, cybersecurity, databases

facts.statement: Big O notation describes the worst-case performance of an algorithm as input size grows
O(1) means constant time: the operation takes the same amount of time regardless of input size
O(n) means linear time: the operation time grows proportionally with input size
O(n^2) means quadratic time: the operation time grows with the square of input size, common in nested loops
O(log n) means logarithmic time: the operation time grows logarithmically, typical of binary search
O(n log n) is the best possible time complexity for comparison-based sorting algorithms like merge sort and quicksort
From fastest to slowest growth: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n) < O(n!)
Space complexity measures how much additional memory an algorithm uses relative to the input size

common_errors.wrong: Big O measures exact running time in seconds
common_errors.correct: Big O describes how running time scales with input size, not the exact time. An O(n) algorithm could be faster or slower than O(n^2) for small inputs.

common_errors.wrong: O(n) and O(2n) are different complexities
common_errors.correct: In Big O notation, constant factors are dropped. O(2n) simplifies to O(n) because they grow at the same rate.

common_errors.wrong: the fastest algorithm is always the best choice
common_errors.correct: A faster algorithm may use more memory or be harder to implement. The best choice depends on the specific constraints and requirements.

facts.statement: Bubble sort repeatedly steps through the list, comparing adjacent elements and swapping them if they are in the wrong order; O(n^2) average case
Selection sort finds the minimum element and places it at the beginning, then repeats for the remaining elements; O(n^2) average case
Merge sort divides the array in half, recursively sorts each half, then merges them; O(n log n) in all cases
Quick sort picks a pivot element and partitions the array into elements less than and greater than the pivot; O(n log n) average case
Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time by inserting each element in its correct position; O(n^2) average but O(n) for nearly sorted data
A stable sort preserves the relative order of elements with equal keys; merge sort is stable, while quicksort is typically not
Binary search finds an element in a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half; it has O(log n) time complexity
Linear search checks each element one by one from start to end; it has O(n) time complexity and works on both sorted and unsorted data

common_errors.wrong: bubble sort is a good algorithm for large datasets
common_errors.correct: Bubble sort has O(n^2) complexity and is very slow for large datasets. Merge sort or quicksort are much faster alternatives.

common_errors.wrong: quicksort is always O(n log n)
common_errors.correct: Quicksort's worst case is O(n^2), which occurs when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element. Average case is O(n log n).

common_errors.wrong: there is one best sorting algorithm for all situations
common_errors.correct: Different algorithms have different strengths. Insertion sort is fast for small or nearly sorted data; merge sort guarantees O(n log n); quicksort is often fastest in practice.

common_errors.wrong: binary search works on unsorted arrays
common_errors.correct: Binary search requires the array to be sorted first. Using binary search on an unsorted array gives incorrect results.

facts.statement: Binary (base 2) uses only digits 0 and 1; it is the fundamental number system used by computers
A bit is a single binary digit (0 or 1); a byte is 8 bits and can represent values from 0 to 255
Hexadecimal (base 16) uses digits 0-9 and letters A-F (A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15)
To convert binary to decimal, multiply each bit by its place value (powers of 2) and add: 1011 = 8+0+2+1 = 11
One hexadecimal digit represents exactly 4 binary bits, making hex a compact way to write binary: FF = 11111111 = 255
1 kilobyte (KB) is approximately 1,000 bytes; 1 megabyte (MB) is approximately 1,000 KB; 1 gigabyte (GB) is approximately 1,000 MB
ASCII is a character encoding standard that represents each letter, number, and symbol as a number between 0 and 127
Unicode is a universal character encoding standard that can represent characters from virtually all writing systems in the world, using up to 4 bytes per character

common_errors.wrong: computers understand human language directly
common_errors.correct: Computers only understand binary (0s and 1s). All data, instructions, and programs are ultimately represented in binary.

common_errors.wrong: binary 10 equals decimal 10
common_errors.correct: Binary 10 equals decimal 2 (1x2 + 0x1 = 2). The same digits represent different values in different number systems.

common_errors.wrong: 1 KB is exactly 1,000 bytes
common_errors.correct: In computing, 1 KiB (kibibyte) is exactly 1,024 bytes (2^10). The SI prefix kilo means 1,000, creating ambiguity that led to the kibibyte distinction.

facts.statement: Boolean logic uses only two values: true (1) and false (0)
AND returns true only when BOTH inputs are true; otherwise it returns false
OR returns true when AT LEAST ONE input is true; it returns false only when both inputs are false
NOT inverts the input: NOT true = false, NOT false = true
XOR (exclusive or) returns true when EXACTLY ONE input is true, but false when both are true or both are false
Logic gates are physical implementations of boolean operations in computer hardware circuits
A truth table lists all possible input combinations and their corresponding outputs for a boolean expression
De Morgan's Laws state that NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B)

common_errors.wrong: OR means one or the other but not both
common_errors.correct: In boolean logic, OR (inclusive or) returns true when either or both inputs are true. XOR (exclusive or) returns true only when exactly one input is true.

common_errors.wrong: AND and OR have the same priority
common_errors.correct: AND has higher precedence than OR in most programming languages and boolean algebra, similar to how multiplication has higher precedence than addition.

common_errors.wrong: boolean logic is only used in programming
common_errors.correct: Boolean logic is used in computer hardware (logic gates), database queries, search engines, digital electronics, and mathematical proofs.

facts.statement: A variable is a named storage location in a computer's memory that holds a value which can change during program execution
An integer (int) is a data type that stores whole numbers without decimal points, such as -5, 0, or 42
A string is a data type that stores a sequence of characters (text), usually enclosed in quotation marks
A float (floating-point number) is a data type that stores numbers with decimal points, such as 3.14 or -0.5
A boolean is a data type that can only have two values: true or false; it is used in conditions and logical operations
An array (or list) is a data structure that stores multiple values in a single variable, accessed by their position (index), usually starting at 0
A constant is like a variable but its value cannot be changed after it is set; constants are used for values that should stay the same, like PI = 3.14159
Type casting (or type conversion) is changing a value from one data type to another, such as converting the string '42' to the integer 42
Variable names should be descriptive and follow naming conventions; most languages do not allow spaces or starting with a number in variable names

common_errors.wrong: a variable's value can never change
common_errors.correct: Variables can be reassigned to new values during program execution. Only constants are values that cannot be changed once set.

common_errors.wrong: the number 5 and the string '5' are the same in programming
common_errors.correct: The integer 5 and the string '5' are different data types. The integer can be used in math operations, while the string is text and cannot be directly used in calculations.

common_errors.wrong: arrays always start counting at 1
common_errors.correct: In most programming languages (Python, Java, C, JavaScript), array indices start at 0. The first element is at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on.

common_errors.wrong: you can name a variable anything you want
common_errors.correct: Variable names must follow rules: they cannot start with a number, cannot contain spaces, and cannot use reserved keywords (like 'if', 'while', 'class').

facts.statement: A conditional statement (if/else) executes different code depending on whether a condition is true or false
A for loop repeats a block of code a specific number of times; it is useful when you know how many times to repeat
A while loop repeats a block of code as long as a condition remains true; it is useful when you do not know in advance how many times to repeat
An infinite loop runs forever because its exit condition is never met; this is usually a bug that can crash a program
Nested loops are loops placed inside other loops; the inner loop completes all its iterations for each single iteration of the outer loop
A break statement exits a loop immediately, even if the loop condition is still true
An else-if (elif) statement allows checking multiple conditions in sequence; only the first true condition's code block is executed
Iteration means repeating a process; each time through a loop is called one iteration
A counter variable is often used in loops to keep track of how many times the loop has executed

common_errors.wrong: a while loop and a for loop do completely different things
common_errors.correct: Both while and for loops repeat code. A for loop is typically used when the number of repetitions is known; a while loop when it depends on a condition. Either can often replace the other.

common_errors.wrong: an if statement always needs an else
common_errors.correct: An if statement can exist without an else. The else block is optional and only needed when you want to execute alternative code if the condition is false.

common_errors.wrong: infinite loops are always intentional
common_errors.correct: Most infinite loops are bugs caused by forgetting to update the loop variable or having a condition that can never become false. Intentional infinite loops do exist (e.g., game loops) but include a break condition.

common_errors.wrong: nested loops always mean the code is wrong
common_errors.correct: Nested loops are a valid and common pattern, used for tasks like processing 2D arrays, generating combinations, or working with grids. They just need to be used carefully to avoid slow performance.

facts.statement: A function is a reusable block of code that performs a specific task; it can accept inputs (parameters) and return an output
A parameter is a variable listed in a function's definition; an argument is the actual value passed to the function when it is called
The return statement sends a value back from a function to the code that called it
A syntax error occurs when code violates the programming language's grammar rules; the program will not run at all
A runtime error occurs while the program is running, such as dividing by zero or accessing a missing file
A logic error produces incorrect results even though the program runs without crashing; the code does not do what the programmer intended
Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors (bugs) in a program; the term originated when Grace Hopper found an actual moth in a computer in 1947
Functions help organize code by breaking a large program into smaller, manageable pieces that can be tested and reused independently
A function call executes the code inside the function; the same function can be called many times from different places in a program
Scope determines where a variable can be accessed; a variable defined inside a function (local variable) cannot be used outside that function

common_errors.wrong: defining a function and calling a function are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Defining a function creates the code but does not run it. Calling (or invoking) a function actually executes the code inside it.

common_errors.wrong: a function can only return one thing, so functions without return values are useless
common_errors.correct: Functions without return values (void functions) are useful for performing actions like printing output, modifying data, or triggering events.

common_errors.wrong: logic errors will always cause the program to crash
common_errors.correct: Logic errors produce wrong results without crashing. For example, using + instead of - gives an incorrect answer but the program runs normally.

common_errors.wrong: print statements and return statements do the same thing
common_errors.correct: A print statement displays output to the screen for the user. A return statement sends a value back to the calling code for further processing; it does not display anything.

facts.statement: The internet is a global network of interconnected computers that communicate using standardized protocols (rules)
A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the address of a webpage, like https://www.example.com
HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) and HTTPS (HTTP Secure) are protocols that web browsers use to communicate with web servers
An IP address is a unique numerical label assigned to each device connected to a network, like a mailing address for computers
DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (like google.com) into IP addresses that computers use to find each other
A web server is a computer that stores and delivers web pages to users; a client is the device (like your phone or laptop) that requests and displays pages
Cloud computing provides computing services (storage, processing, software) over the internet instead of on a local computer
The World Wide Web (WWW) was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989; it is a system of interlinked pages accessed via the internet, but it is not the same as the internet itself
Bandwidth measures how much data can be transmitted over a network connection per second, typically measured in Mbps (megabits per second)

common_errors.wrong: the internet and the World Wide Web are the same thing
common_errors.correct: The internet is the global network infrastructure (cables, routers, protocols). The World Wide Web is a service that runs on the internet, using browsers to access web pages.

common_errors.wrong: WiFi is the internet
common_errors.correct: WiFi is a wireless technology that connects devices to a local network router. The router then connects to the internet. WiFi without an internet connection cannot access websites.

common_errors.wrong: the cloud is an actual cloud in the sky
common_errors.correct: Cloud computing uses large data centers (buildings full of servers) located around the world. 'The cloud' is just a metaphor for accessing remote computers over the internet.

common_errors.wrong: deleting something from your device permanently removes it from the internet
common_errors.correct: Content posted online may have been copied, cached, or archived by other servers. Deleting from your device only removes your local copy.

facts.statement: A strong password should be at least 12 characters long and include a mix of uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols
Phishing is a type of cyberattack where criminals pretend to be a trusted source (like a bank or friend) to trick people into revealing personal information
Malware is malicious software designed to harm or exploit computers; types include viruses, worms, trojans, ransomware, and spyware
Encryption converts data into a coded form that only authorized users can read; HTTPS uses encryption to protect data sent between your browser and websites
Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second layer of security beyond a password, such as a code sent to your phone or a fingerprint
A firewall monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on security rules, acting as a barrier between a trusted network and untrusted networks
Personal information that should be protected online includes full name, address, phone number, passwords, Social Security number, and financial information
A computer virus is a type of malware that attaches itself to a program and spreads when that program is run, similar to how biological viruses spread
Software updates often contain security patches that fix vulnerabilities; keeping software updated is an important cybersecurity practice

common_errors.wrong: only big companies get hacked, not individuals
common_errors.correct: Anyone can be a target of cyberattacks. Individuals are frequently targeted through phishing emails, malware, and identity theft.

common_errors.wrong: using the same password for everything is fine if it is a strong password
common_errors.correct: Using the same password everywhere means if one site is breached, all your accounts are compromised. Use unique passwords for each account.

common_errors.wrong: a firewall protects against all types of cyberattacks
common_errors.correct: Firewalls primarily control network traffic. They do not protect against phishing, social engineering, insider threats, or malware downloaded by the user.

common_errors.wrong: Macs and iPhones cannot get viruses
common_errors.correct: While less commonly targeted, Apple devices can and do get malware. No device is completely immune to security threats.

facts.statement: A database is an organized collection of data stored electronically that can be easily accessed, managed, and updated
A relational database organizes data into tables (like spreadsheets) with rows (records) and columns (fields)
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language used to create, read, update, and delete data in relational databases
A primary key is a unique identifier for each record in a database table; no two records can have the same primary key
A query is a request for specific data from a database; for example, 'find all students with a grade above 90'
Data can be sorted (arranged in order), filtered (showing only items that match criteria), and searched in a database
Databases are used everywhere: libraries track books, schools store student records, stores manage inventory, and websites store user accounts
A backup is a copy of data stored separately in case the original is lost or damaged; regular backups are essential for data protection

common_errors.wrong: a database is just a spreadsheet
common_errors.correct: While both organize data in rows and columns, databases support multiple related tables, enforce data integrity rules, handle millions of records efficiently, and allow concurrent access by many users.

common_errors.wrong: SQL stands for 'Sequel' with no meaning
common_errors.correct: SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is sometimes pronounced 'sequel' but the letters stand for specific words describing its purpose.

common_errors.wrong: deleting data from a database always means it is gone forever
common_errors.correct: If proper backups exist, deleted data can often be restored. Many database systems also have transaction logs that can recover recent changes.
